newsitem.title: SPAIN: New EU-harmonised CPI index to favour Spain - INE.
newsitem.headline: New EU-harmonised CPI index to favour Spain - INE.

text.p: Spanish inflation in January was still one-tenth above European Union (EU) single currency requirements and among the EU's highest rates despite a new calculation method that worked in its favour.

National Statistics Institute INE said on Friday that the publication of the EU's new harmonised index was good news for Spain as the methodology had increased inflation rates in the three best performing countries.

Decisions on whether a member state meets the single currency inflation requirement will be based partly on the harmonised Consumer Price Index (CPI), published for the first time on Friday for January 1997.
The Maastricht Treaty requires nations to have a yearly inflation rate not more than 1.5 percentage points higher than the average of the three best performing member states.
"This is a very good news for all Spaniards," said INE president Maria Pilar Martin-Guzman at a news conference.
She presented a table with January data where Spain, together with its neighbour Portugal, stands at 2.8 percent -- a decimal point above the European threshhold for the month of 2.7 percent.
In January, the only other country above that level was Greece with 6.6 percent.
The main effect of the new methodology was to push values for Sweden and Finland higher, which with Luxembourg are the leaders for among the EU's 15 members.

Sweden sees its domestic index value of minus 0.1 percent rise to a positive 1.3 percent according to the new harmonised index, while in Finland the new calculation pushes CPI up to 0.9 percent from the 0.6 percent domestic figure. Luxembourg remains unchanged.
"Our domestic index was a very good one, as is proved by the fact that the new methodology did not change it a lot," Martin-Guzman said.
She added that the 1996 time series proves that the differential between the domestic index and this new harmonised figure was never higher than one decimal point.
The two indices produced exactly the same values for the months May to September.
"That does not mean that the index won't produce bigger differences in the future," she warned.
Compared with the domestic index, the new harmonised data is keeping out some items linked to health and teaching services.
INE said it would continue to publish its usual domestic figure for the time being.
It added there has as yet been no decision on whether the harmonised figure would be announced from each country separately or all together from Eurostat.

Other countries' CPI, such as Great Britain and Portugal, were reduced even more than Spain's by the new methodology. For January, Portugal's CPI is 3.3 percent according to the domestic figure and 2.8 percent according to the new index.
